cases.name: code reviewer finds correctness/security/test risks first
cases.scenario: A future edit weakens the Mesh-Talk code-review agent. Evaluate whether the prompt still forces prioritized, evidence-backed review findings for a Rust/Tauri encrypted messenger.
rubric: Requires review of the diff or PR scope before judging unrelated code.
Prioritizes correctness and security before style.
Requires test coverage or regression-test assessment.
Requires concrete file:line style findings and actionable suggestions.
Forbids inventing findings when the diff is clean or unverified.

cases.name: e2e runner executes and triages real backend E2E
cases.scenario: A future edit changes the E2E runner prompt. Evaluate whether it still runs real mesh-talk-node multi-process tests and reports only evidence-backed green/failure states.
rubric: Requires running make e2e or the equivalent ignored multi-process Rust tests.
Explains startup timeout, process death, delivery assertion, and multicast environment triage.
Requires rerun or clear evidence before classifying flakes.
Requires per-test verdict and exact failure evidence.
Forbids claiming green unless the test output was observed.

cases.name: bug hunter reports only verified correctness/security bugs
cases.scenario: A future edit makes the bug-hunter prompt more speculative. Evaluate whether it still demands verified bugs, concrete repros, and severity.
rubric: Requires verified findings, not speculative style complaints.
Focuses on Mesh-Talk high-risk surfaces: parsers, crypto, sync, relay, transport, and account/device routing.
Requires repro input or event sequence for every confirmed issue.
Requires severity, blast radius, and fix direction.
Keeps the agent read-only.

cases.name: project agent rules preserve validation and architecture context
cases.scenario: A future edit weakens repo-level agent guidance. Evaluate whether the rules still identify project structure, core modules, testing layers, build commands, and security constraints.
rubric: Lists core Rust modules and Tauri/frontend structure.
Documents make test, make e2e, frontend e2e, and check-health entry points.
Identifies architecture docs before crypto, sync, or transport changes.
Requires networking/crypto changes to ship integration assertions.
Includes security and quality gate expectations.

cases.name: delivery eval runbook makes real and deterministic gates explicit
cases.scenario: A future edit removes key runbook detail. Evaluate whether the runbook still distinguishes deterministic smoke, real smoke, real AI eval, trigger rules, known gaps, and human review.
rubric: Names the deterministic smoke command and the real AI eval command.
Names full real smoke commands for backend and frontend workflows.
Explains local, CI, PR, Codex, and Claude Code triggers.
States when human review is still required.
Does not claim model-output quality is proven without running a model-backed eval.

cases.name: post-office privacy documentation states the actual trust boundary
cases.scenario: A future relay change or documentation edit overstates metadata privacy. Evaluate whether the design document accurately describes what a post office can and cannot learn or guarantee.
rubric: Explains which original event fields are encrypted and which outer routing fields stay visible.
States that authenticated connections, timing, counts, and size buckets can expose communication patterns.
States that the relay can withhold or delete events and that several relays do not replicate custody.
Discloses the lack of metadata forward secrecy under later static device-key compromise.
Explains that V1 clear-header copies are not retroactively hidden and may require sender retry.
Distinguishes tested behavior from privacy guarantees that require a different protocol.

cases.name: post-office macOS service runbook is operable and protects credentials
cases.scenario: An operator installs or updates the headless post office on an Intel Mac. Evaluate whether the runbook supports a safe, verifiable service lifecycle and states its limits accurately.
rubric: Names the installed binary, data, logs, LaunchAgent, and listening/discovery ports.
Keeps the keystore password out of process arguments and the plist, and requires owner-only password file permissions.
Gives reproducible build, update, health, and restart commands without discarding queued events or identity.
Explains that a LaunchAgent runs only in the logged-in user's GUI session.
States that other relays do not replicate queued events and identifies remaining routing metadata exposure.
Provides an executable cross-machine delivery test that stops the sender before the recipient returns.

Separately verifies a relayed offline file offer and encrypted file bytes recovered from the relay after its restart with the sender stopped; explains that recipient consent still requires direct overlap with the sender.

cases.name: post-office Windows service runbook is operable and protects credentials
cases.scenario: An operator installs or updates the headless post office on Windows. Evaluate whether the runbook supports a safe, verifiable Scheduled Task lifecycle and accurately distinguishes the cross-machine test layers.
rubric: Names the Windows binary, data directory, Scheduled Task identity, and TCP and UDP ports.
Keeps the keystore password out of process arguments and restricts relay data access to SYSTEM and Administrators.
Gives reproducible build, install, update, health, and restart commands that preserve queued events and the relay identity.
Explains stale lock recovery after a task restart and requires evidence that the service is listening.
Separately tests offline DM and channel delivery, file offer, complete encrypted file bytes, and multi-relay election against the installed Windows relay.
States that recipient consent needs sender overlap, queued custody is not replicated, and routing metadata remains exposed.

cases.name: routed discovery and bridge document keeps network and identity boundaries clear
cases.scenario: A user runs A and B on one LAN, C on another, and E as a post office on A and B's LAN. Only C and E have an existing Tailscale connection. Evaluate whether the document explains what is required for bidirectional Mesh Talk discovery and messaging without promising arbitrary LAN bridging.
rubric: Says Mesh Talk never installs, configures, or authorizes Tailscale and treats its addresses only as candidates.
Requires signed discovery and Noise identity verification before an endpoint is trusted for communication.
States that E is bridge-enabled, A/B/C explicitly opt in, and A/B do not need Tailscale when they can reach E over LAN.
Explains that the directory shares self-signed short-lived introductions and cross-LAN encrypted DMs travel through E's opaque mailbox rather than IP subnet forwarding.
States that the bridge is default off, invisible nodes do not participate, and disabling it ends local participation.
Does not promise WebRTC media, arbitrary TCP forwarding, or delivery while E is unavailable.

cases.name: two post-office gateways preserve identity and mailbox limits
cases.scenario: A/B use E on LAN X and C/D use F on LAN Y. Only E and F can reach each other through an existing Tailscale connection. Evaluate whether the documented solution supports cross-LAN peer discovery and encrypted DMs without implying relay-to-relay mailbox replication or subnet bridging.
rubric: States that both post offices require an explicit pinned bridge-peer configuration and must use distinct TCP ports.
Says clients opt in to bridge discovery and learn the remote relay through the authenticated local bridge directory.
Requires a fresh signed remote relay proof and end-to-end Noise authentication through the TCP gateway.
Explains that participating clients register with every reachable verified relay and use a local relay first unless they set an optional preference.
States that relay mailbox contents are not replicated and inter-site delivery needs a surviving route between the sites.
Provides real cross-machine evidence covering all four client identities and bidirectional encrypted DMs.
